title: The Pizza Tracker: We've Been Trained to Pay for Fake Progress Bars
dek: Domino's pizza tracker started as an internal management tool, then became a global app standard. It works because it turns waiting into visible work; and once companies discovered we love watching progress bars, they started faking them.
why: Medium information density, but the second half about 'deliberate slowdowns' and 'fake progress bars' is valuable. Suitable for listeners interested in product design and consumer psychology.
who: Product managers, designers, founders building consumer apps, and anyone wanting to understand 'progress bar psychology'.
skip: The first two minutes about Planet Money's book and game, asking for reviews, can be skipped.

points.h: The 30-minute guarantee sold control, not speed
points.body: Domino's once promised delivery in 30 minutes or it's free. That guarantee made drivers speed, leading to deaths and lawsuits, and it was eventually dropped. But David Halbenstricker has a theory: the guarantee was popular not just because it was fast, but because it gave customers a sense of control. In the early 2000s, Domino's commissioned a study and found that customers' psychology after ordering pizza is a rollercoaster: the peak is at order time, then it slides downhill—'Where's my pizza? Did they lose my order?' No matter the actual wait, what customers hate is the waiting process.

points.h: Internal tools had to work first, then customer-facing
points.body: Company executives didn't want to build a pizza tracker at first because tracking every pizza at every store was too time-consuming and seemed like a gimmick. What they were really obsessed with was 'out-the-door time.' A UK franchisee used a monitor to display out-the-door times from five to ten nearby stores, letting them compete, and gave cash rewards to top-ranked stores. David's boss visited the UK and had David replicate the system in the US. David connected each store's out-the-door time to a central system, creating a real-time dashboard. The CEO said it was the thing that most drove performance during his tenure.

points.h: The tracker was a byproduct of the internal system
points.body: David and his colleague realized they already had a system tracking every pizza, so they decided to 'hitch a ride' and build a customer-facing tracker. In 2006, most people didn't have smartphones; FedEx, UPS, and Amazon could track packages, but on a scale of days, not minutes. Real-time pizza progress tracking was entirely new. The designer drew an interface like a horizontal thermometer, from order, prep, bake, box, to delivery, with each completed step turning the next segment red. When David saw the design, he said: 'This is a hot dog. We're a pizza company, why put a hot dog?' But executives liked it and decided to launch before the Super Bowl.

points.h: Designers use the pizza tracker as a meeting prop
points.body: Shuya Gong was a design director at IDEO and later taught design at Harvard. In the mid-2010s, she consulted for many companies and found one of the most effective meeting openers was to order a pizza on the spot, project the tracker on a big screen, and ask the client: 'How do you feel right now?' She said you can feel anxiety rising or falling in your body very intuitively, feel reassurance and groundedness. Then you can ask: which parts do you want your users to feel when using your product? The pizza tracker became a shorthand in her design circle: whenever a client involves waiting, say 'they need a pizza tracker.'

Shuya said one reason the pizza tracker is popular is that as shopping experiences become more digital, the tracker replicates an important part of the physical world—watching others work. Online experiences lack this visibility, so people get impatient more easily. Researchers found that reminding customers of the labor behind a product makes them value it more, calling it the 'labor illusion.' Shuya also mentioned a more mysterious mechanism: the tracker changes our perception of time. Like walking somewhere, the return trip feels shorter because it's familiar and has landmarks. The pizza tracker gives us familiar routes and landmarks—pizza being made, on the way, being delivered—making the wait feel shorter.

points.h: Banks deliberately slow transfers to fake waiting
points.body: In the mid-2010s, Shuya worked with banks and fintech companies and found their problem was the opposite of Domino's: customers weren't used to transfers being too fast. Two computers talk, confirm the amount, and the money is gone—no road to cross, no cheese to melt. But for people used to money taking a while to arrive, instant transfer 'feels suspicious.' So companies deliberately slow down the 'money tracker,' not giving real-time feedback but adding a buffer to make you wait. Shuya said this is intentionally slowing down time, adding meaningful friction, so you feel the seriousness and weight of the transfer while waiting. The host asked: isn't this advising lying to customers? Shuya said she prefers to understand it as 'curating the experience,' adding back the physicality that existed in traditional experiences to make people comfortable.

points.h: TurboTax and Uber progress bars may be fake
points.body: TurboTax shows an animation during tax filing saying 'We're checking your deductions and credits.' But a few years ago someone checked the code and found the animation is the same for everyone, in all situations, and takes the same time. The question is: does TurboTax want to reassure us during the terrifying tax process, or use the labor illusion to make us feel paying a lot is worth it? Uber is similar: the host repeatedly received updated pickup times, but the car almost always arrived later than promised. It felt like the tracker was part of a deliberate deception to make you choose Uber over Lyft, to keep you from canceling, to make you stand on the street early. The show contacted TurboTax and Uber; TurboTax didn't respond, Uber didn't arrange an interview but shared some data suggesting their pickup times are quite accurate.

points.h: Field test: the pizza tracker is mostly real
points.body: Nick biked to a local Domino's to stake out, while Alex ordered a half-Hawaiian half-pepperoni pizza at home and monitored the tracker in real time. Nick ordered another pepperoni pizza in the store as cover. The tracker showed 'Ivan' making the pizza, but when Nick asked the employee's name, he said 'Alex.' The tracker also showed 'quality check,' but Nick didn't see any quality inspector. However, David explained that because Domino's uses conveyor ovens, bake time is almost fixed, so the tracker automatically jumps to the next step after a set time. Eventually, the pizza came out, was boxed, and was driven away by Alex (aka Ivan), with Nick biking after, almost mistaken for a stalker. Alex pressed 'delivered' at Nick's door, and the tracker updated quickly. Conclusion: the tracker is mostly accurate, but 'Ivan making' and 'quality check' are fake.

terms.def: Reminding customers of the labor behind a product makes them value it more.
Domino's internal metric: the time from order to when the pizza leaves the store.
Domino's real-time order progress bar launched in 2006, widely imitated since.

quotes.text: It was a story about how an IT department of a pizza restaurant completely changed how we wait and how we feel when we wait.
We already have a system tracking every single pizza and every single Domino's. We went, ah, we can piggyback on that and do pizza tracker.

It doesn't actually take that much time for two computers to talk to each other and say, like, is this the amount of money that we're sending over? Yes, this is the amount of money we're sending over.

And so what we would do in that instance is actually slow down the pizza tracker, the money tracker. And instead of giving you a real-time reflection, we might actually give it a little bit of a buffer and make you wait.
How much are we recommending lying to your customers?

Because we've gotten so used to these kinds of apps that helped us transition to the digital world, holding our hands step by step to show us that some work was really happening, that now in our totally digital lives, we want that feeling even when it's completely disconnected from reality.
